TechNova Solutions — Employee Handbook
 Fictional sample knowledge-base document | Version 1.0
Document notice: All company names, policies, processes, and examples in this document are fictional and created
solely for software testing and demonstration.
1. Working principles
TechNova Solutions is a fictional organization used to demonstrate document retrieval. This handbook describes
illustrative workplace expectations. Employees are expected to act respectfully, communicate clearly, protect
customer and company information, and raise concerns through appropriate channels. The handbook supplements,
but does not replace, the sample HR Policies document.
2. Professional conduct
Employees should treat colleagues, customers, vendors, and visitors with courtesy. Harassment, discrimination,
intimidation, retaliation, and abusive conduct are not acceptable in this fictional workplace. Concerns may be

parent_1.page_content:
reported to a manager, HR, or the designated confidential reporting channel. Reports should be handled discreetly
and reviewed by an appropriate person. Retaliation against someone who raises a concern in good faith is prohibited
under this sample standard.
3. Communication and meetings
Teams should use the approved collaboration platform for work discussions and keep decisions discoverable.
Meeting organizers should provide an agenda when practical, invite only relevant participants, and record decisions
and action items. Employees should distinguish confirmed decisions from proposals. Sensitive employee or
customer information should not be posted in broad channels. For urgent incidents, use the incident escalation
process rather than relying only on an ordinary chat message.
4. Information handling
Company information should be classified according to its sensitivity. Public information may be shared externally

parent_2.page_content:
when approved. Internal information is intended for employees and approved contractors. Confidential information,
including customer records, credentials, employee records, and unreleased business plans, must be shared only
with authorized recipients using approved systems. Employees must not place passwords or API keys in source
code, tickets, public repositories, or chat messages.
5. Equipment and acceptable use
Company devices are provided primarily for business use. Employees should install software only from approved
sources and should not disable endpoint protection or security controls. Lost or stolen devices must be reported
promptly to the IT service desk. Personal devices may access company systems only when permitted by the
applicable security standard. Employees should lock their screens when away from their workstations.
6. Conflicts of interest and outside work
Employees should disclose a situation that could reasonably create a conflict between personal interests and

parent_3.page_content:
company responsibilities. Examples include evaluating a vendor owned by a close relative, using confidential
information for personal benefit, or accepting an improper gift. Outside employment or consulting should be disclosed
when it may affect working hours, confidentiality, or business interests. HR and the employee's manager determine
the appropriate review path.

parent_4.page_content:
7. Questions and acknowledgement
Questions about workplace expectations should be directed to the employee's manager or HR. Employees should
acknowledge receipt of the current handbook through the designated HR portal. Acknowledgement confirms receipt;
it does not mean that every illustrative example applies in every jurisdiction or circumstance.
End of sample document.

parent_5.page_content:
TechNova Solutions — HR Policies
 Fictional sample knowledge-base document | Version 1.0
Document notice: All company names, policies, processes, and examples in this document are fictional and created
solely for software testing and demonstration.
1. Purpose and scope
This document describes sample human-resources policies for the fictional company TechNova Solutions. It is
designed as test content for an information-retrieval application. It is not an actual company policy, employment
contract, or legal guidance. These sample rules apply to hypothetical full-time employees unless a section says
otherwise.
2. Annual leave
For this fictional example, full-time employees receive 20 working days of annual leave per calendar year. Annual
leave is credited monthly at the rate of 1.67 days, with rounding handled by the HR system. Employees should
submit planned leave requests through the employee portal at least five working days before the first day of leave. A

parent_6.page_content:
manager reviews requests based on team coverage, project deadlines, and previously approved leave. A request is
not approved until the employee receives confirmation in the portal. Employees should not assume that submitting a
request means it has been approved.
3. Sick leave
The sample policy provides 10 working days of paid sick leave per calendar year. Employees who are unwell should
notify their manager as soon as reasonably practical, preferably before their scheduled start time. For an absence of
more than three consecutive working days, HR may request appropriate supporting documentation, subject to
applicable law and company procedure. Medical details should be shared only through approved confidential HR
channels, not in public team chats.
4. Remote and hybrid work
Eligible teams may use a hybrid schedule with up to three remote working days per week, subject to role
requirements and manager approval. Employees working remotely must be reachable during their agreed core

parent_7.page_content:
hours, protect confidential information, and use company-approved devices and access methods. A manager may
require onsite attendance for customer meetings, planning sessions, training, or operational needs. Remote work
from another country requires prior written approval because of security, tax, and employment considerations.
5. Public holidays and attendance
The company publishes a holiday calendar for each employee location. Employees should consult the calendar
assigned to their work location. If a public holiday falls on a weekend, any substitute day is determined by the
published calendar and local requirements. Employees should record working hours and absences accurately in the
attendance system. Corrections should be submitted to the manager and HR within five working days of noticing an
error.
6. Leave escalation and questions
If an employee believes a leave balance is incorrect, the employee should first review the balance and transactions

parent_8.page_content:
in the HR portal. If the discrepancy remains, the employee should raise an HR service request with the relevant
dates. For an urgent leave matter, the employee should contact the manager and HR through the approved internal

parent_9.page_content:
channel. The HR team owns interpretation of this fictional policy and records approved exceptions.
End of sample document.

parent_10.page_content:
TechNova Solutions — IT Support and
 Troubleshooting Guide
 Fictional sample knowledge-base document | Version 1.0
Document notice: All company names, policies, processes, and examples in this document are fictional and created
solely for software testing and demonstration.
1. How to raise an IT request
Employees should submit an IT service request through the support portal and include the affected device,
application, time the issue began, exact error message, and troubleshooting steps already attempted. Do not include
passwords, authentication codes, or secret keys in a ticket. Select the category that best matches the issue so that
the request reaches the correct support queue.
2. Network connectivity
If a device cannot reach an internal service, first check whether the device is connected to the approved network or
VPN. Confirm that other trusted websites or services are reachable. Restarting the approved VPN client may resolve

parent_11.page_content:
a temporary connection problem. If the issue continues, record the time, network type, error message, and whether
other applications are affected. Do not bypass network controls or install unapproved tunneling software.
3. Account access and multi-factor authentication
If sign-in fails, verify that the username is correct and that the device clock is synchronized. Check whether the
account is locked or whether the password has expired. For multi-factor authentication problems, use the approved
account recovery process. Support staff should verify the requester's identity before changing authentication
settings. Never share a one-time passcode with another person, including someone claiming to be from IT support.
4. Software installation
Employees should request software through the approved software catalogue. The request should state the
business purpose and the device on which the software is needed. Administrators review licensing, security, and

parent_12.page_content:
compatibility before approval. Users should not download installers from unknown websites or disable endpoint
protection to complete an installation.
5. Device performance
For a slow device, note when the slowdown occurs and whether it affects one application or the entire system. Check
available storage and close unnecessary applications. Install operating-system updates through the approved update
mechanism. Do not delete managed security tools or unknown system files. If the device becomes unusually hot,
repeatedly crashes, or shows signs of compromise, stop using it for sensitive work and contact IT support.
6. Incident escalation
Suspected malware, lost devices, exposed credentials, or unauthorized access should be reported immediately
through the security incident channel. Include the time discovered and a factual description of what happened. Do
not attempt to investigate by opening suspicious attachments or deleting potential evidence. The security team will

parent_13.page_content:
provide containment instructions and coordinate follow-up.
End of sample document.

parent_14.page_content:
TechNova Solutions — RAG and Retrieval Guide
 Fictional sample knowledge-base document | Version 1.0
Document notice: All company names, policies, processes, and examples in this document are fictional and created
solely for software testing and demonstration.
1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, is an application pattern in which a system retrieves
relevant external information and supplies it to a language model when generating an answer. The retrieved material
can ground the response in a selected knowledge base. RAG does not guarantee correctness: retrieval can miss
relevant evidence, documents can be outdated, and a language model can still misinterpret context. Systems should
expose source information and evaluate retrieval quality.
2. Document ingestion
A typical ingestion workflow loads source documents, extracts text, normalizes metadata, splits text into chunks,

parent_15.page_content:
creates searchable representations, and stores the records. Useful metadata can include document name, page
number, section heading, source identifier, and ingestion timestamp. Keeping source metadata makes it easier to
trace a retrieved passage back to its origin.
3. Chunk size and overlap
Chunk size controls the maximum length of a text segment, while chunk overlap repeats a small portion of text
between adjacent segments. Smaller chunks can improve retrieval precision for focused questions but may omit
surrounding context. Larger chunks preserve more context but can introduce irrelevant text and consume more
prompt tokens. Chunk size should be selected through evaluation rather than treated as a universal constant.
4. Parent-child retrieval
A parent-child retrieval design indexes smaller child chunks while retaining larger parent sections in a separate
document store. Search operates over the child chunks. Each child stores a parent identifier. After retrieving a

parent_16.page_content:
matching child, the application uses that identifier to fetch the corresponding parent section and supplies the larger
context to the language model. This approach combines fine-grained matching with broader context. The parent
store must preserve stable identifiers and support reliable lookup.
5. Dense and sparse retrieval
Dense retrieval represents text and queries as embedding vectors and finds semantically similar items. It can match
related concepts even when the wording differs. Sparse retrieval, such as BM25, uses term statistics and is useful for
exact keywords, names, identifiers, and rare terms. Hybrid retrieval combines the complementary strengths of dense
and sparse search. The application should normalize or fuse ranked results rather than assume raw scores from
different methods are directly comparable.
6. Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines ranked result lists using each result's position rather than comparing the

parent_17.page_content:
raw scores produced by different retrieval systems. A common formulation adds 1 divided by a rank constant plus
the result rank for each list in which a document appears. Documents ranked highly by multiple retrieval methods
receive stronger combined scores. The implementation should use a stable document identifier to recognize the
same item across result lists.

parent_18.page_content:
7. Reranking and context compression
A reranker evaluates query-document relevance for an initial candidate set and produces a revised ordering. A
common pipeline retrieves a broader set of candidates, reranks them, and keeps a smaller number for generation.
Context compression aims to reduce irrelevant material in the final prompt. Reranking and compression can reduce
noise and token usage, but the selected passages must still preserve enough evidence to answer the question.
8. Retrieval evaluation
A retrieval system should be evaluated with representative questions and known relevant source passages. Useful
measures include recall at k, precision at k, mean reciprocal rank, and latency. End-to-end answer evaluation should
also check factual support, citation accuracy, and whether the answer abstains when evidence is insufficient. Record
retrieval, reranking, and generation latency separately to identify bottlenecks.
End of sample document.

parent_19.page_content:
TechNova Solutions — Technical Operations Guide
 Fictional sample knowledge-base document | Version 1.0
Document notice: All company names, policies, processes, and examples in this document are fictional and created
solely for software testing and demonstration.
1. API authentication
Internal services should authenticate using approved credentials such as scoped API keys or OAuth access tokens,
depending on the service. Credentials must be stored in a secret manager or protected environment configuration.
Do not hard-code credentials in source files, commit them to Git, or include them in application logs. Rotate a
credential immediately if exposure is suspected. Use the minimum permissions required for the service's task.
2. HTTP request practices
Clients should set explicit connection and read timeouts. They should validate response status codes and parse
response bodies defensively. A successful HTTP response does not guarantee that the returned business data is

parent_20.page_content:
complete, so applications should validate required fields. Retry only operations that are safe to repeat. For retryable
failures, use bounded exponential backoff with jitter and respect any Retry-After header.
3. Error handling
Applications should distinguish client errors, server errors, network failures, and validation failures. A 400 response
generally indicates an invalid request; a 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication; a 403 indicates insufficient
permission; a 404 indicates that the requested resource was not found; and a 429 indicates rate limiting. A 5xx
response indicates a server-side failure. Error messages returned to end users should be useful without exposing
stack traces, secrets, or internal infrastructure details.
4. Logging and observability
Logs should include a timestamp, severity, service name, and correlation identifier where available. Avoid logging

parent_21.page_content:
passwords, access tokens, personal data, or complete confidential request bodies. Metrics should capture request
count, error rate, and latency. Distributed traces can help identify which service contributes to end-to-end delay.
Retention and access to logs should follow the organization's approved security and privacy controls.
5. Configuration management
Applications should read environment-specific configuration from environment variables or a configuration service. A
local .env file may be used for development, but it must be excluded from version control. A .env.example file should
document variable names with placeholder values only. Validate required configuration at application startup and fail
with a clear message when a required setting is missing.
6. Deployment and change management
Changes should be reviewed before merging into the main branch. Automated tests should run before deployment.

parent_22.page_content:
Deployments should have a rollback procedure and a record of the version released. Database or index schema
changes should be planned so that the running application and stored data remain compatible. Production
credentials must be separated from development credentials.
End of sample document.
